rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes to the first four; no to the fifth. The relevant duty is Article 53(1)(b): a provider of a general‑purpose AI model must draw up, keep up‑to‑date and make available to providers of AI systems intending to integrate the model information and documentation that enables them to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and to meet their own obligations, containing at a minimum the elements in Annex XII (Article 53(1)(b)(i), (ii)). Date of release, yes. Annex XII.1(c) requires the date of release together with the methods of distribution. Number of parameters, yes. Annex XII.1(f) requires the architecture and number of parameters. Applicable model interaction with hardware, yes. Annex XII.1(d) requires how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself, where applicable; the qualifier "where applicable" means the item is owed whenever such interaction exists, and Annex XII.2(a) separately requires the technical means (instructions for use, infrastructure, tools) needed to integrate the model into AI systems. Licence, yes. Annex XII.1(h) requires the licence for the model. Samples of outlier data used in training, no. Annex XII.2(c) requires only information on the data used for training, testing and validation, where applicable, including the type and provenance of the data and the curation methodologies; it does not require samples, records or exemplars of any data, outlier or otherwise. Outlier detection appears only as an example of data‑cleaning methodology in Annex IV.2(d), which is the technical documentation for high‑risk AI systems and does not bind a GPAI‑model provider under Article 53(1)(b). The separate Article 53(1)(d) duty is likewise a sufficiently detailed public summary of training content according to the AI Office template, not the disclosure of data samples. Two qualifiers complete the answer. First, Article 53(1)(b) applies without prejudice to the need to observe and protect intellectual property rights and confidential business information or trade secrets, so the manner of disclosure may be shaped by that proviso, but it does not delete the Annex XII minimum items. Second, under Article 53(2) the Article 53(1)(a) and (b) obligations, and hence the whole Annex XII disclosure to downstream providers, do not apply to models released under a free and open‑source licence allowing access, use, modification and distribution, whose parameters, including weights, architecture and model‑usage information, are made publicly available; that carve‑out is lost where the model is classified as a general‑purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51, in which case all four items become owed again regardless of licence.

Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: Healthcare decision-making is not itself one of the areas of high-risk use cases; Annex III contains no "health" or "healthcare" heading, although several of its listed use-cases and the separate Annex I product route do capture particular health-related systems. The eight areas listed as numbered headings in Annex III, to which Article 6(2) attaches high-risk classification, are: biometrics (in so far as their use is permitted under Union or national law); critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement (in so far as their use is permitted under Union or national law); migration, asylum and border control management (likewise so far as permitted); and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III, points 1 to 8). Only a lettered use-case under one of those headings makes a system high-risk under Article 6(2), the heading alone does not. Health-related systems therefore become high-risk only where they fall within a listed use-case or the product route. Under Annex III, point 5, that covers AI systems used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them (point 5(a)); risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance (point 5(c)); and evaluation and classification of emergency calls, dispatch or dispatch-prioritisation of emergency first response services including medical aid, as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems (point 5(d)). Separately, under Article 6(1) an AI system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, which is how clinical AI within medical devices and in vitro diagnostic medical devices is caught (Annex I, points 11 and 12). Clinical decision support that sits outside both routes is not high-risk by virtue of its subject matter alone. Conversely, an Annex III system is not high-risk under the Article 6(3) derogation where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making, and one of four conditions is met: it performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use-case, but it is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons. The Commission may add or modify Annex III use-cases by delegated act under Article 7(1) only where the system is intended to be used in one of the areas already listed and poses a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, equivalent to or greater than that of the systems already listed, so a new health use-case would have to be attached to an existing area rather than to a new one.

No

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Adding guardrails does not move a system out of the high-risk class, and the Regulation contains no "moderate risk" classification into which it could be moved. Changing the system's capabilities and intended purpose, by contrast, can change the classification, because classification is driven by intended purpose and function, not by residual risk after mitigation. Classification under Article 6 is binary and purpose-based. On the Annex I route (Article 6(1)), a system is high-risk if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral law. On the Annex III route (Article 6(2)), a system is high-risk if its intended purpose falls within one of the lettered use-cases under the eight areas of Annex III. Neither test asks how well the risk is controlled. Guardrails are instead the consequence of that classification: Article 8(1) requires compliance with the Section 2 requirements taking into account the intended purpose and the state of the art, and Article 9 requires the provider to identify and analyse known and foreseeable risks, estimate risks arising under reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluate post-market monitoring data, and adopt targeted risk-control measures. A guardrail is an Article 9 mitigation discharging the obligation, not evidence that the obligation never attached. The same holds for an agentic system's autonomy: autonomy is an assessment criterion under Article 7(2)(d) for the Commission's delegated-act power, and a factor in the Article 9 analysis, not a lever a provider can pull to self-declassify. The only in-Regulation route by which an Annex III system escapes high-risk status is the Article 6(3) derogation: the system must pose no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and must fulfil one of four conditions, it performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use-case. The derogation is unavailable, and the system is always high-risk, where it performs profiling of natural persons. The provider must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service. Note that the four conditions describe what the system does, not what it is prevented from doing, so guardrails only assist where they genuinely confine the system's function to one of those roles, which is a change of capability and intended purpose rather than a bolt-on safeguard. Changing capabilities and intended use therefore is the operative lever. Because Article 6(1) turns on the system being a safety component of an Annex I product and Article 6(2) turns on the intended purpose falling within an Annex III use-case, a genuine redefinition that removes the system from the safety-component function or from the listed use-case removes the classification. The change must be real and documented, not a disclaimer: the intended purpose, and the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, must be stated in the instructions for use (Article 13(3)(b)(i)), together with the level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 13(3)(b)(ii)) and any known or foreseeable circumstance related to use in accordance with the intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse which may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights (Article 13(3)(b)(iii)). Article 9(2) requires the reasonably foreseeable misuse of the narrowed system to be assessed on its own terms, so a purpose restriction that the system's capabilities do not actually enforce will not survive that assessment. The directional asymmetry matters for whoever makes the change. Article 25(1) makes a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party a provider subject to the Article 16 obligations where they put their name or trademark on a high-risk system, make a substantial modification to a high-risk system such that it remains high-risk under Article 6, or modify the intended purpose of a system not classified as high-risk so that it becomes high-risk under Article 6. There is no corresponding provision converting a downgrade into a change of role; a narrowing modification simply means the Article 6 test is reapplied to the modified system on its own facts, with the actor making the modification bearing the documentation burden. Finally, altering the risk level of a category is a Commission power, not a provider's. Article 7(1) lets the Commission amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases only where both conditions are met cumulatively, the systems are intended to be used in an area already listed in Annex III, and they pose a risk of harm to health and safety or an adverse impact on fundamental rights equivalent to or greater than that posed by the systems already listed. Article 7(3) lets the Commission remove a use-case only where both the system concerned no longer poses any significant risks to fundamental rights, health or safety having regard to the Article 7(2) criteria, and the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection under Union law. Notably, the availability of effective measures to prevent or substantially minimise risks is an Article 7(2)(k)(ii) criterion in that Commission-level assessment, which confirms that mitigation quality is a legislative input to the list, not a self-assessment defence against it. Any such amendment is made by delegated act subject to the Article 97 conditions, including expert consultation and the non-objection period. For a general-purpose AI model, the parallel point is that Article 51(2) presumes high-impact capabilities where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations, and Article 51(1)(a), (b) otherwise turns on high-impact capabilities evaluated against technical tools, indicators and benchmarks, or a Commission decision having regard to the Annex XIII criteria. Output filters and usage policies do not alter training compute; only a genuine capability difference, evaluated on those bases, bears on that classification, and a Commission decision remains the route under Article 51(1)(b).
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states that the EU AI Act does not have a 'moderate risk' classification and that the derogation in Article 6(3) is binary, thus satisfying the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly lists and explains the four conditions in Article 6(3), emphasizing that exemption depends on the system's intended task meeting one of them.
The answer confirms that changing the system's capabilities and intended use can remove high-risk status if the new purpose satisfies one of the Article 6(3) conditions.
The answer explicitly states that systems performing profiling of natural persons are always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or changes to intended use.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is allowed, but it must be disclosed, and no lighter regime applies to it. Nothing in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 prohibits generating synthetic clinical images for teaching. Article 5(1) contains an exhaustive list of eight prohibited practices, manipulative or deceptive techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities based on age, disability or socio-economic situation, social scoring, individual criminal-risk profiling based solely on personality traits, untargeted facial-image scraping for recognition databases, emotion inference in workplaces and education, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, and illustrative image generation engages none of them. Note only that Article 5(1)(f) does bar emotion-inference systems in educational institutions, which is a separate matter from content generation, and that under Article 5(8) the Article does not affect prohibitions arising under other Union law, which remains relevant if the synthetic dermatological images are derived from identifiable patient photographs. Nor does the use become high-risk: the education area of Annex III covers admission and allocation, evaluation of learning outcomes, assessment of the appropriate level of education, and monitoring of prohibited behaviour during tests, and producing teaching illustrations is not one of those listed use-cases, so Article 6(2) is not triggered. The transparency duty does apply. A photorealistic AI-generated image of a skin condition on a human subject is a "deep fake" within Article 3(60), AI-generated or manipulated image content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, precisely because its pedagogical value lies in students taking it to be a faithful clinical presentation. The university, using the system under its own authority in a professional capacity, is the deployer under Article 3(4) and is therefore bound by Article 50(4), first subparagraph, to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Under Article 50(5) that information must be given in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first exposure, in practice, a marking on the slide, image caption or course materials at the point the image is shown. The law-enforcement carve-out is not a lighter standard and does not apply. Article 50(4), second sentence, is a complete exemption from the deepfake disclosure duty, and it is confined to use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, "law enforcement" as defined in Article 3(46). Teaching is outside it. The separate exemptions in Article 50(4), fourth subparagraph, authorised criminal-law use, or content that has undergone human review or editorial control with a natural or legal person holding editorial responsibility, attach only to the duty on AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest; academic review or faculty sign-off of the images therefore does not excuse the deepfake disclosure. The only attenuated regime is in Article 50(4), third subparagraph: where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, transparency is limited to disclosure of the existence of the generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. A medical teaching image is presented to students as an accurate representation of a real clinical sign rather than as a fictional or artistic creation, and educational illustration is not "analogous" to the artistic, creative, satirical and fictional categories listed; the rationale of that subparagraph, protecting the aesthetic experience of a work, has no counterpart here, and clear labelling in no way impairs the teaching use. Full disclosure under the first subparagraph is accordingly required. Two related points complete the position. If the university merely uses a third-party generator, the provider of that system bears the Article 50(2) duty to mark outputs in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, subject to that paragraph's own limits for systems performing an assistive standard-editing function or not substantially altering the deployer's input data or its semantics, and for legally authorised criminal-law use. If instead the institution develops or has developed and puts into service such a generator under its own name, it assumes those provider duties itself. Finally, Article 50(6) confirms that these transparency obligations do not affect the requirements in Chapter III, though as analysed no high-risk classification arises on these facts.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is allowed, aligning with the substance that such use is not prohibited under Article 5(1) or other provisions.
The answer explicitly confirms the applicability of the disclosure obligation under Article 50(4) for deep fake content, even in educational contexts.

The answer rejects the applicability of the lighter transparency regime, arguing that educational illustration is not analogous to artistic or fictional works, contrary to the criterion's assertion that it does apply.
The answer correctly identifies that the law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and explicitly states it does not apply to educational use.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On the facts given, this is not a high-risk AI system, and it is not a prohibited practice either. The "resembles policing" argument fails because Annex III's law-enforcement area (Annex III, point 6) is drawn by use-case and by actor: it covers AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies in support of them) for the listed purposes such as risk assessment of offending or re-offending, polygraphs, evidence reliability evaluation and criminal-analytics profiling. A supermarket operating a loss-prevention tool on its own premises is a private deployer pursuing its own commercial and property interests, not an entity acting on behalf of a law enforcement authority, and a staff bag check is not a criminal investigation or prosecution. Resemblance to investigating theft does not import an Annex III heading; only a use-case actually listed in Annex III makes a system high-risk under the Annex III route, and none of the other seven areas, biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, migration/asylum/border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes, is engaged by current-cart and checkout anomaly detection. The separate Annex I route is also unavailable: the tool is not a safety component of, nor a product covered by, Union harmonisation legislation. The "evaluation or classification leading to detrimental treatment" argument likewise fails. Article 5(1)(c) prohibits social scoring only where an AI system evaluates or classifies natural persons or groups over a certain period of time on the basis of their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, and the resulting social score leads to either or both of: (i) detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the context in which the data was originally generated or collected, or (ii) detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. Here the analysis is confined to the current cart and the checkout event, no accumulation over time, no personality inference, no cross-context use, and the consequence (an optional manual bag check at the same till, in the same transactional context that generated the data) is neither unrelated-context treatment nor, on its face, disproportionate to the conduct flagged. Article 5(1)(d) is also not triggered. It prohibits AI systems making risk assessments of natural persons to assess or predict the risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics, and it expressly does not apply to AI systems used to support the human assessment of a person's involvement in criminal activity where that assessment is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to criminal activity. The tool assesses concrete checkout anomalies in the transaction itself, objective, verifiable facts, and feeds a human decision on whether to conduct a check; it does not predict future criminality from profiling or personality traits. The stated absence of biometrics, face recognition and sensitive-trait inference likewise keeps Article 5(1)(f) and (g) and the remaining prohibitions out of scope. Two conditions would change this. First, if the system in fact retains and aggregates behaviour across visits or customers to build a persistent risk or "trust" score, or if flags feed consequences beyond the checkout, loyalty-account penalties, store bans, sharing with other retailers, the Article 5(1)(c) limbs become live. Second, if the output ceases to support a human assessment grounded in observable transaction facts and instead predicts a propensity to offend, Article 5(1)(d) applies and the derogation is lost. As described, the system falls outside the prohibitions and outside both high-risk routes, leaving the retailer with the Article 4 AI literacy duty and, where the output is presented to customers or staff, general Union law on data protection and non-discrimination.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as its unambiguous position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explains that Annex III.6 applies only to systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, stating the substance of the criterion.
The answer explicitly states that a supermarket operating a loss-prevention tool is a private deployer not acting on behalf of law enforcement, thus falling outside Annex III.6.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No. Opting out of the third‑party conformity assessment does not release you from Chapter III, Section 2, on the contrary, the opt‑out is lawful only if you have covered those very requirements by standards. Article 43(3) governs high‑risk AI systems covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I. Its first subparagraph states that the provider follows the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure, that the requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III apply to those systems, and that they shall be part of that assessment; points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply, and notified bodies notified under the sectoral act may control conformity with Section 2 where their compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed in the notification procedure. Its final subparagraph addresses the operator's situation exactly: where a Section A act enables the manufacturer to opt out from a third‑party conformity assessment on condition that it has applied all harmonised standards covering all the relevant requirements, that manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III. The opt‑out is therefore conditional, not exculpatory, the very fact that the Regulation regulates it confirms that a system meeting Article 6(1)(a) and (b) remains high‑risk and that Section 2 continues to bind you; what changes is only the route by which conformity is demonstrated, from notified‑body involvement to the operator's own application of standards. Practically, that means risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record‑keeping, transparency to deployers, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity must all be satisfied and evidenced through the standards you invoked; if no harmonised standard or common specification covers a given Section 2 requirement, the sectoral opt‑out is unavailable to you. Article 43(4) further requires a new conformity assessment upon any substantial modification, excluding changes pre‑determined by you at the initial assessment and documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV for systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer unambiguously states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing the relevant provision and explaining its effect.

The answer clearly explains that the opt-out is conditional on applying harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements, not just sectoral ones, directly reflecting the substance of the criterion.
